text: Vietnam now has nearly 16.5 million elderly people (aged 60 and above), putting the country among those with the fastest-aging population in Asia.
It is forecast that, by 2034, their number will swell to nearly 21 million.

As a result, Vietnam's "golden population" period is expected to end around 2036, and it must use the decade left to prepare for the upcoming "aging population" period, with one of the top priorities being the development of a "silver economy".
Also known as the "gray economy" - the silver economy refers to all activities, products, and services designed and operated to meet the needs of the elderly.

Vietnam's silver economy actually began to form some time ago, but it was spontaneous and fragmented due to the absence of a comprehensive national development strategy, and primarily consisted of services for the elderly, typically represented by elderly care centers, excluding State-owned social protection centers.
The issue at hand nowadays is the need to develop the silver economy on a national scale, led and oriented by the State, with a comprehensive and long-term development strategy.

This must not only serve the elderly according to social security policies but also create opportunities and conditions for healthy older individuals with the means, capacity, and expertise to directly participate in its development, thus contributing to the country's socio-economic development while mobilizing the participation of businesses and economic sectors so that it truly becomes an important pillar of social security policies and an integral part of the national economy.

The "Silver Economy in Vietnam in the New Era" seminar, organized by the Vietnam Association of the Elderly in collaboration with the Central Commission for Policy and Strategy, the Ho Chi Minh National Academy of Politics, and the Communist Review in November 2025, contributed to a unified understanding of the importance of population aging, which is not just a challenge but also an opportunity for development.
The elderly are not only beneficiaries of policies but also resources for and drivers of development.

Based on this, six major directions were identified to build a project for the development of Vietnam's silver economy by 2035, with a vision to 2045, which is expected to be submitted to the Politburo in the first quarter of 2027, including directions for institutional improvements; encouraging economic sectors to participate; expanding international cooperation; promoting science, technology, and digital transformation; and linking the development of the silver economy with social security.

Subsequently, a conference on the development of the silver economy worldwide and the adaptation of Vietnam's policies and strategies, chaired by the Prime Minister on March 11, 2026, also clearly defined the roles of stakeholders in the silver economy ecosystem, with elderly people at the center; businesses as the core of innovation and implementation; and the State as the creator of institutions, guiding and leading development.

Developing the silver economy is not simply about expanding and improving the quality of elderly care services; it requires a renewal of development thinking, institutional systems, and governance models to proactively create an economic model that aligns with the country's development requirements in the new era.
The policy for developing the silver economy is clear.
The question is how to transition from awareness to action to turn it into concrete results?
To provide additional information on the silver economy development project, our Cover Story in this edition features a series of articles analyzing the ecosystem required in Vietnam.
Dr. CHU VAN LAM CHAIRMAN OF THE EDITORIAL BOARD
